That with respect to income of corporations earned on and after January 1, 1953, for the present rate of tax of 20 per cent on the first $10,000 of taxable income and 50 per cent on taxable income in excess of $10,000 there be substituted the rate of 18 per cent on the first $20,000 of taxable income and 47 per cent on taxable income in excess of $20,000.

That for the 1953 and subsequent taxation years a taxpayer whose principal business is production, refining or marketing of petroleum or petroleum products or exploring or drilling for petroleum or natural gas or mining or exploring for minerals and who, having entered into an agreement on or after January 1, 1953, to pay an amount, other than a rental or royalty, to a government to acquire the right to take oil, gas or minerals from land in Canada, has paid all or part of the amount and before a well or mine comes into production on the land surrenders the right without receiving consideration therefor or repayment of any part of the amount so paid, be allowed to deduct the amount so paid in computing income for the year in which the right is surrendered.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
We are now dealing with
paragraph 6 of the Income Tax Act amending resolutions.

Mr. Chairman, I presume
the parliamentary assistant will assure us that the basis of calculating the period in question in arriving at the amount of medical expenses will be the same as at present, namely a 12 months' period ending in the calendar year in question?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: That is right.

I am sure the committee
welcomes this proposal. It is one that can claim popularity in all parts of the House of Commons, although it does not go as far as the house indicated it would have liked in a memorable vote a year ago. Nevertheless this is a step in the right direction and one which I am sure will be welcomed.
However, because it is not complete in that respect I should like briefly to renew the plea that has been made by others and by myself in other years with respect to categories of medical supplies and those other things that are admitted under the present regulations and the present act within the definition of medical expenses.
I say to the parliamentary assistant, as I have said to the minister for some years, that I cannot see any justification for treating hearing aids as deductible medical expenses but denying a similar recognition to aids to seeing. There is no distinction in principle at all. I renew the plea that aids to sight, namely eyeglasses, should be included within the scope of allowable medical expenses.
Then I should like to renew the plea that was advanced in other years in regard to drugs. At present the number of drugs 68108-199i
Income Tax Act
treated as allowable medical expenses is narrowly limited. If it be proper to admit some drugs within this category, then I fail to see on what principle other drugs should be excluded. We in the house are familiar with the distinction that has existed for some time as between drugs prescribed by medical practitioners in the country and those prescribed in the city. We realize that in the country a prescription is usually filled by the medical practitioner and the cost included in his bill. In cities the practice is to have medical practitioners' prescriptions filled by pharmacists; and in that case it has been the practice for many years to reject claims based upon such expenditures.
I am urging that where drugs are used- and in many cases these are extremely expensive drugs-they should be permitted as deductions. A year ago four drugs were admitted within the charmed circle of allowable medical expenses. Some of us mentioned other extremely expensive drugs which are required by persons who are chronic sufferers from certain diseases. Notwithstanding the heavy medical expenses they have to pay, and regardless of the extent of the expense they may incur for drugs prescribed for their use, no allowance whatever is made for them. I think that is a situation which is not only unfair but highly discriminatory.
Last year in the amendments to this act the principle was admitted that at least the expenditures on four drugs should be regarded as deductible medical expenses. I suggest the same should be done in connection with expenditures made on other drugs, particularly those in the expensive category such as are required by chronic sufferers.
Let me say in conclusion that while we welcome this as a step in the right direction, in that it is a reduction from 4 per cent to 3 per cent of taxable income as the amount permitted to be subtracted for medical expenses before arriving at the net taxable income, nevertheless it is only a step, and there are anomalies still existing which I think it is the duty of this parliament to remove.

May I say that I concur in the remarks of the hon. member for Eglinton. We are happy to see the reduction from 4 per cent to 3 per cent, but of course we are not satisfied with that. We think the floor should have been removed, and the house hoped and suggested it would be removed when the vote was taken some time ago.
I do not propose to go over the arguments again, but I do say that I hope as time goes on this floor will be removed. In fact I hope that sooner or later, and the sooner

Income Tax Act
the better, we shall have a national health plan so we will not require legislation of this kind to either lower or raise the floor under medical expenses.
The burden of health services, particularly medical aid, is becoming so great that the average individual cannot carry the load. I am not blaming the medical profession; I am not blaming the hospitals; I am not blaming the nurses or any of those others who are engaged in giving the services required by those who are ill. They do an admirable job, as I have good reason to know. But of necessity the cost is going up. I know that some of the equipment used in hospitals and by medical men in their offices, but used infrequently, requires a heavy investment. That heavy investment has to be retired, or has to be considered when charging for the services that are rendered through its use.
Then with regard to drugs and other necessary pieces of equipment such as eyeglasses, I agree with what the hon. member for Eglinton has said. It is true that in the larger centres those who buy expensive drugs cannot deduct them under the present system, but those who live in the country are able to do so when the drugs are provided by the medical man.
We welcome this reduction in the floor, but we would have liked to have seen it wiped out completely. I believe that in the not too distant future all forms of health services will have to be made available to the individual whether he can afford to pay for them or not. In other words, this should be part of a general social security plan. Of course it would be set up by this parliament but be administered by the local authorities. No one wants to centralize this and put the whole thing under the control of the federal authorities. It must be on a co-operative basis, much as the old age pensions were brought in in 1926.
The hon. member for Peace River will probably make his annual plea in connection with vitamin E. I do not want to trespass on his territory but to say that we are warmly in support of any representations he may make in that regard.

I should like to support the last two speakers who have requested that special drugs and eyeglasses be included in the deductions. I should like also to make a plea in connection with charges for ambulance service. I understand that if the doctor pays for the ambulance and puts the charge on his bill it is deductible. In my riding there are a number of people who must be taken to Toronto at least once a month for special treatment, and when they go by ambulance they are faced with a charge
[Mr. Coldwell.l
of $25, $30 or $35, with the same thing for the return trip. There are other places even farther away from any large medical centre. I think consideration should be given to allowing legitimate ambulance costs as a deduction, and provision therefor should be made in this resolution.

First I should like to indicate my support of what has been said by all three of the speakers who have preceded me. Nothing has been said with which I could disagree. The appeals made to the minister and his assistant have been good and to the point. I do hope we are coming to the time when the government will give favourable consideration to the appeals being made by members on every side of this house to remove completely the floor under medical expenses. We do not want to see this 3 per cent provision continued at all. People from one end of this country to the other want to be able to deduct all medical expenses from their taxable income.
As was mentioned by the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar, for several years I have appealed to the government to place on the tax free list such medicines as di-alpha tocopherol which have now become of general use in the treatment of heart diseases and certain circulatory troubles. Year by year the use of this drug has been extended and it has proved to be of great benefit to a large number of sufferers.
But the cost is rather high. Sometimes it runs to as much as 75 cents a day for those who are suffering from certain types of heart trouble.
I should like to have the parliamentary assistant indicate what is the government's policy with respect to the placing of medicines on the tax free list. How does a medicine get there? We have been making appeals in connection with these substances for some years. If the criteria is widespread use and widespread recognition by medical practitioners that the substance is valuable, then it seems to me that these vitamin E products should have been on the tax free list long before this. Can the parliamentary assistant give us some idea just what is the policy, and how we would go about getting this substance on the tax free list?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
I was going to wait until all hon. members who wanted to say something had spoken. I do not want to go over all the arguments that have been given time and again by the Minister of Finance and my predecessor. The policy of the government as given by the minister will be found no later than January 12 of this year, as reported on page 900 of Hansard.

The list of drugs and other deductible items is constantly under review in the light of administrative difficulties that would be encountered. Rome was not built in a day and this list, along with many others, is getting longer all the time. While I am speaking only for myself and am not announcing government policy, I am sure that the list of drugs will be added to as time goes on.
There are certain administrative difficulties in connection with these vitamin E products and as to what should be exempt. Shall we exempt just the pure vitamin E or anything that contains vitamin E? It would be easy to put out a product containing just a little vitamin E. If the hon. member for Peace River has some way of resolving that difficulty I am sure the officials of the department will be only too delighted to discuss the matter with him.

I appreciate the statement made by the parliamentary assistant. I may say that he is doing a good job and I am sure he will listen when I tell him of a very easy way by which this could be done. I should like to see him give this his earnest and early consideration. I do not suggest allowing into Canada free of duty any drug that contains vitamin E, but there is one substance known as concentrated di-alpha tocopherol which is manufactured only in Rochester, New York. This substance is distilled from wheat germ and comes into Canada in concentrated form. It is not an oil at all. It is extracted from the oil. It can easily be identified; and since it comes from only one corporation and is brought into Canada by not more than three or four importers-

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: But we are not talking about duties now.

-it would be a simple thing to deal with it on a tax free basis. If it is not an oil product and only comes in as concentrated tocopherol then it should be easy to deal with as such. There are only three or four companies in Canada that are importing it and that incorporate it into capsules for administration to sick people. It should not be any more difficult to deal with than the substances that are being used for the treatment of arthritis and which are on the tax free list.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
I thank the hon. member for
all the information he has given us, and I assure him that the officers of the Department of Finance and the Department of National Revenue will take up the matter with the officers of the Department of
Income Tax Act
National Health and Welfare and study it very carefully.
Thank you very much.

I rise to support the hon. member for Peterborough West in his plea for some latitude with respect to what is included in medical expenses. He mentioned particularly ambulance services. I am interested in that by reason of the fact that a year or two ago I had a case which I brought to the attention of the government but in which the claim was not allowed. This gentleman's wife was ill and had to be taken to a specialist. The specialist was in Calgary and this man lived in the Crows-nest pass area. The ambulance had to travel a distance of almost 200 miles. I know that if the doctor had included the ambulance account in his bill and had paid it, it might have been exempt, but doctors are reluctant to include such accounts in their bills when they have to pay them from their own pocket and take a chance on getting the money from the patient.
There is another point that is of importance here. Ambulance bills are bills that have to be paid. Otherwise those running the ambulance companies would go broke. An ambulance is a piece of machinery involving the use of gas and oil to operate it and the wages of the operator and perhaps an assistant. These charges have to be paid. While I think the medical profession is sometimes pretty well paid, yet I will say that generally speaking they are quite magnanimous in their attitude toward poor people who cannot always pay their bills. Very often doctors will reduce their bills. I know of one case where a doctor had to perform an operation on an old age pensioner and the bill for the operation was in the neighbourhood of $200. I got in touch with the doctor and told him that this person was an old age pensioner and there was not a chance in the world of him paying the bill. The doctor said he did not know that the individual was an old age pensioner, and he cut his bill in half.
By the way, that was not in Alberta. It happened to be in another province. Doctors often do cut their bills to patients, but an ambulance company will not do that because it is a somewhat different type of service. Nevertheless it is absolutely necessary sometimes for patients to have ambulance service, and I believe the bills for such services should be included in the medical expenses that are exempt.
Before the parliamentary assistant replies I should like to ask him one further question. I am in full agreement with other people

Income Tax Act
who have spoken that all medical expenses should be exempt. We have supported that. However, the government has only seen fit to bring in this measure reducing the floor from 4 per cent to 3 per cent. Has the government given any thought to a graduated scale of exemptions on the basis of income? I ask this question because I think a fairer method could be worked out. Sickness is no respecter of persons. It comes to rich and poor alike.
I know the government will say that is why they have it on a percentage basis, but let us look at it this way. Take the case of a single man. He has a certain income and of course there is the chance that he will be taken ill and have to undergo an operation with the result that at the end of the year he will have a medical bill. On the other hand, let us consider the case of the married man, of course with a wife, who has four children. In that family there are six people. We will say that this man receives the same income as the single fellow. But the chances of sickness in that home and the chances of incurring medical expenses are six times as great as in the case of the single person receiving the same income.
I am wondering whether the government has given any consideration to a graduated scale, for example, let us say 1 per cent for incomes up to $2,000, 2 per cent for incomes from $2,000 to $3,000, 3 per cent for incomes from $3,000 to $4,000 and 4 per cent for incomes from $4,000 to $5,000, something after that fashion. I do not necessarily mean that those should be the figures. It would be fairer to a man in the lower income bracket, particularly a married man with a family, to have a larger exemption for medical expenses than the more fortunate individual. Has the government given any consideration to that? When the parliamentary assistant replies I should like him to give an answer with respect to the two questions, ambulance services and the matter of a graduated form of exemption.

It is not my intention to go over the ground I covered the other day when I spoke on the budget, but I should like to ask the parliamentary assistant if the department will give consideration to three main points. One of them has some relation to the remarks just made by the hon. member for Macleod. I think the question of a graduated scale could be covered very easily, and without using a graduated scale, by the application of the floor. Therefore I should like to make my first request the matter of such application and ask the parliamentary assistant if the department will consider

applying the 3 per cent floor to the taxable income of the taxpayer rather than to the net income. In that way the taxpayer will reap the benefit of his marital status and dependents, as the case may be.
The second request is that the department give consideration to permitting deduction of medical expenses expended on behalf of a deceased dependent for a reasonable period of time after the death of the dependent. I would suggest perhaps two years.
The third request is that the department also consider permitting taxpayers to make deductions for properly vouched medical expenses on behalf of relatives who are not properly classified as dependents of the taxpayer.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I can assure the hon. member for Macleod and the hon. member for Hamilton West that consideration is constantly being given to the problems they have just mentioned; and more attention will be given since they have brought them up in the house.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Shall we pass on to
paragraph 7?

No, Mr. Chairman. I would
like an answer about the ambulance question.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: I just gave it. I said that these items are constantly under review in the light of administrative difficulties, but that greater consideration would be given since the matters have been raised by the members of the house at this time.

I would like to bring to the attention of the parliamentary assistant and the department a problem which has been drawn to my attention. It is that a cerebral palsy centre which provides training for such unfortunate children is not known as a registered hospital. The expenses of treatment of a child taking training at a centre like that are not allowed for income tax purposes and subject to the medical floor allowable, because the institution is not classified as a hospital. I trust the department will give serious consideration to allowing expenses connected with cases of that kind to be deducted, subject to the floor that is now in effect. We do know that the Department of National Health and Welfare of this government, as well as the government of Ontario, contribute to centres such as I have mentioned, but the contributions are not sufficient to take care of the patients. For that reason I hope serious consideration will be given to this request.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
I thank the hon. member for
drawing that particular matter to the attention of the department. You may rest

assured that we shall look into it. I was just discussing the situation with our good friend the Minister of National Revenue who, being a doctor, knows much about the matter.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Shall we go on to the
next paragraph?
Agreed.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: No. 7.

This deals with expenses
for higher education and I am glad to see it included in the resolutions. In my opinion, however, it does not go far enough.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
May I interrupt the hon.
gentleman and tell him that I was going to ask the Minister of National Revenue to move the following amendment:
That before the last two words of the resolution, "a university", there be inserted the words "a school or".

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue
speechtext: I would so move.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
The committee has heard
the amendment. Shall it carry?
Carried.

That is a slight help, but the point I wish to make concerns something on which I have spoken in this house before.
A taxpayer putting the members of his own family through a university, particularly in medicine, engineering, law or any of the other sciences-which take about a seven year course nowadays-is required to expend very, very considerable sums on that education in the higher echelons of the education process. I have always thought it was most unfair that a taxpayer should not be allowed to deduct those expenses from his income in computing his income tax.
If a taxpayer gives a scholarship to a university, up to 10 per cent of his total income, that scholarship is allowed as a deduction. On the other hand, if he obligates himself to the very much more essential job of educating his own children, in the field of higher education, up to now he has received no allowance for it.
I would assume that this provision means that an exemption of $400 is allowed per child or per dependent going to a school, university or place of higher learning, after the age of 21 years. I am not complaining or saying that it is not some help; but with respect to university education there are fees and, frequently, the expense of a dependent living away from home. A taxpayer today undertakes a very considerable financial burden in order to put his children through for any of the professions. It is my contention, Mr. Chairman, that everything should be
Income Tax Act
done to encourage the taxpayer to undertake this onerous duty toward his own family.
I would like to see this regulation enlarged in the future so that the total expenses, fees charged at the university and fees charged at the school, would be deductible from income for taxation purposes. I most earnestly make that plea, Mr. Chairman, to the parliamentary assistant.

Mr. Chairman, I support the previous speaker in his request, and I am very happy to have heard the amendment that has been made just now. The term "school", however, can be interpreted in a very wide manner, and I hope it is interpreted to embrace as wide a scope as possible. I would like the minister, if he can, to elaborate on just what is meant by the term "school", as I have had one or two requests in that regard. Perhaps because I happen to be one of the trustees of a theological institution, when this was first brought out in the budget speech I received quite a number of requests for some explanation. Does this apply to theological seminaries? The institution with which I happen to be connected is not affiliated with a university, but it does give a course that is equal to any theological course given in a university, and it also grants a degree.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Is it a night school?
No, it is a day school. I should like to ask if this section would apply to young people who are supported by their parents while they are training for the ministry or for missionary work.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Is it on a full-time basis?
Yes.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Then it is covered.

If they are going out in the
profession, is that the general principle?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: It covers bona fide students on a full-time basis in theological schools.
What about vocational schools?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: What is a school? It is a place of learning. Is not a theological school a place of learning?
Yes.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Well, it is included. To avoid further questions, I would say that nursing schools are included in the definition of a school. This question has been asked by many members.
What about vocational schools?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: They are covered.

This clause covers any school that is giving a full-time course?

Income Tax Act

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
Exactly, and for full-time
students. The student has to be a full-time student.
Would that include a school for the teaching of chiropractics?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
If the student is a full-time
student and it is a place of learning, yes.

I think the hon.
member should study this principle carefully. On the one hand we hear members wanting a reduction in taxation, and on the other hand they want to subsidize students so that every young man of 21 may go to school full time and the government will subsidize him. It is a good principle, but it is beginning to slop over. Why should anyone in Canada have to subsidize a school for preachers in Los Angeles? I cannot see it. I think we should go carefully along this line and not injure the cause we have before us by being overgenerous.

I disagree with the member for Cariboo, who has just spoken, in so far as he considers this assistance to the student as being subsidization of schools or education generally. I just want to say that as I go along, because I suppose someone in this group would be expected to say a word on this particular clause. I have nothing to say on it except a word of commendation. I think I will be credited in this house with having made efforts on various occasions to get grants for education, as such, from any source whatever, so perhaps I would be expected to compliment the government upon clause 7, which I welcome. I believe I may welcome it on behalf of the complete group of which I form a part.

There should not be any
confusion about assisting schools or universities through this measure. It is obviously something for the assistance of the poor parents of the dependent child, and has no reference to a university or school whatever. As a matter of fact arguments could be advanced for assistance to universities and schools, but they could not come within the scope of this resolution.
What limitation is placed upon the word "dependent"? We have cases of boys who earn money during the summer, and we are all interested in that. Some of us have boys going into the north country working in the Labrador iron mines, or British Columbia or somewhere else, who are earning fairly substantial amounts as compared with 10 or 15 years ago, and yet not nearly enough to meet the cost of education. If a boy earns $400 or $500, does he cease to be a dependent for the purposes of this measure?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
The Minister of Finance
announced in the budget speech that from now on a dependent can earn up to $750 and still be considered a dependent.
May I ask, then, if that means all dependents or just those attending schools?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: It means all dependents.

Will that be covered by
regulation?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
It is covered by regulation;
the regulation has already been amended.

Would it include the case of
a dependent mother?	.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: It would, of course, because "dependent" covers the case of all dependents.
That is unless-

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
We are now discussing the
regulation which says that a dependent is still a dependent even if he earns up to $750. This regulation is completely distinct from this resolution, which is confined to dependent children.

I should like to refer the parliamentary assistant to his definition of a school. I presume that anyone attending an institution that would give training equivalent to that of a university would be covered by this section. I am referring to the schools of creative arts such as music and singing, which were recognized by the Massey commission investigating the arts and sciences as being equivalent to universities in recognition for scholarships and fellowships. I should think they would get the same recognition here.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: A full-time student of a conservatoire-you know what that is, a place where they teach singing and music-would fall within the scope of this resolution.

That might not be an apt definition, because the student could not be there all day getting lessons. He would get perhaps one or two lessons a week, and then he would spend the rest of the time practising.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: This covers a full-time student. Each case will have to be examined in the light of its particular circumstances. I am sure the officials of the government want to be fair, and we will do whatever is possible to carry out the intention that is behind this resolution. It will be applied with the utmost fairness.

I should like to ask a question about the amendment allowing members

of municipal councils to deduct their expense allowances from income for taxation purposes, as well as members of provincial legislatures-

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: They were covered in 1946.
Can the parliamentary assistant tell me whether all provinces have expense accounts for their provincial legislators?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: I cannot answer that question.
What is the proportion of the total money received that can be regarded as expenses in this case? Is it one-third of the total amount?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Of the money received?
Of the total money received, what proportion of it can be assigned as expenses as opposed to straight salary; shall we put it that way?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: It cannot be divided if it has not been paid as an expense allowance. It has to be paid as an expense allowance, and the amount of expense allowance which is deductible must not be more than half the salary or indemnity which the councillor or mayor receives. It is the same rule as the one we have for members of parliament. Our indemnity is $4,000, and we are entitled to $2,000 tax free expense allowance. The rule is the same, and it is the same for the provincial legislators.
To clarify it, I was directing my original statement to the fact that it could be up to one-third of the total amount, including salary plus expenses.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: If it is paid as such, yes.

Some municipalities
describe the remuneration which is paid to councillors in different ways. In some instances the term used indicates expenses or some sort of an amount to indemnify the councillor for expenses incurred. In other cases it is different. I do not believe we have any places in Ontario, at any rate, where it is actually called a salary, though it may be called an indemnity in some instances.
As I understand it this clause must be adopted by the municipality itself in conjunction with provincial regulations. Is it possible for the municipality so to amend its laws or its regulations to bring them into conformity with this clause? In respect of indemnities paid from 1946 on, must they be specifically named? Must they name the amount paid as expense money in 1946, 1947, 1948, 1949 and 1950 in order to qualify, or can they say now that a portion of that 68108-200
Income Tax Act
amount was considered to be expense money in those years?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: The hon. member is correct in her assumption. It must have been paid as an expense allowance and not be more than half the amount received as salary or indemnity.
I presume, then, it is a matter for the local administration to decide as to what portion was considered to be expense money in those years?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: No, that is not enough. They cannot change what has been done. For instance, if the mayor received $1,000 indemnity and $500 as an expense allowance which was not admitted by the income tax administration, he can now have the $500 in question admitted and he may be reimbursed for his income tax which he has already paid; but it had to be paid to him at that time in the form which I have just mentioned, namely $1,000 as salary, indemnity or whatever you call it, but $500 specifically as an expense allowance.

I should like to ask this question. Let us take county councils. They have their travelling expense which is different for different councils, and they have other expenses. Would they get credit for half of that?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
If the council reimburses
them for their expenses they could deduct them at any time as ordinary expenses. Well, they were reimbursed; they do not have to claim them. The money received was not income. If they have expenses connected with going to the meetings of the council, if they are considered as expenses by the council, clearly council will reimburse them.

Just on that point, I have
some difficulty in understanding the exact meaning. If a municipal body pays its mayor or reeve a certain fixed sum as indemnity and then allows him a certain fixed sum, say 50 per cent of that, as expenses, you may run up against this situation. The mayor may have to come to Ottawa to see the federal government, and he is reimbursed. That is all right. That is not charged against him in his income tax.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
That is not an expense for
him; it is an expense of the municipality. It does not go into his return at all for income tax purposes.
That is fine; that is the answer I want to get.

An indemnity paid
to a legislator is not a salary. It is a sum

Income Tax Act
of money paid to indemnify him against expenses incurred attending the legislature. We seem to assume now that it is a salary and that it is subject to income tax. If the indemnity is too high it should be reduced; but I do not see any sound reason why an income tax should be imposed upon an indemnity paid to a member of a legislative assembly, or any other parliamentary body. It is false, wholly false. The premises are not sound. If the member is paid too much by way of indemnity then it should be reduced, but to tax the indemnity is to suggest that the man receives a salary when attending these places. That is not sound and it is not a fact.
What would be required to show the amount of expenses paid to a member of the provincial assembly or to a member of council? Would there have to be a minute of council or part of a civic act or what?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: A certified extract of the bylaws of the municipality.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: We shall now deal with paragraph 9.
Would a minute of the council itself be sufficient?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Well, a copy of the document that authorizes the payment, whatever it is; a bylaw or resolution, as long as it is certified.

This is going to be a rather tangled up piece of legislation to administer. When I listened to the parliamentary assistant first I thought it was all right. Take a town that pays its mayor $3,000 a year as salary. It is a part-time job. When he is obliged to leave town his expenses are paid by the town, apart from that $3,000. As I heard the parliamentary assistant's first explanation I assumed that that mayor would receive that amount of money by way of salary and that he could automatically write off up to 50 per cent of the salary as an expense account as an offset for taxes. In that way it would be very simple to administer.
You are going to find a thousand municipalities with a thousand different ways of remunerating their mayors and their councils. How the inspector of taxes in any district, who has fifty different decisions to make on that particular item, is going to work it out,
I do not know. If you are correct in your answer to the hon. member for St. John's East that the town or the municipality must have a minute of the council authorizing a certain amount by way of expenses, if it is going to be administered in that way then it is impossible of administration. For the 
provincial legislature it is all right, because a certain percentage of their indemnity is tax free. That is clear. Under this act they can write that off as an offset to income tax.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: No, they do not mention it at all in their income tax returns, any more than you mention the $2,000 that you receive.
That is all right; that is clear.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: It is easy; you do not mention it.

Now you are going into municipalities with it, and you are going to get all kinds of different administrations. I gave you an example of a mayor who draws $3,000 a year as salary; but in addition to that he is paid his expenses if he is obliged to be on the road away from home, or any expenses he may incur in or around the town. I judge from the first explanation that when he is filing his income tax return that sum is the same as the indemnity of a member of the House of Commons or of the legislature. He can omit 50 per cent of his income by way of salary.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: No.
Then I say that the thing is impossible of administration.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
No, I am sorry. The hon. member has not got it right. If there is a bylaw of the council of the municipality under which the person is entitled to a lump sum as an expense allowance, this sum cannot exceed half of any remuneration he gets. If he has no remuneration and no salary he cannot claim a sum for expenses.
The example given by the hon. member is where there was an indemnity or salary of $3,000. If the council decided to allow him an additional $1,500 as expense allowances, the mayor will report the $3,000 he has received and, in lieu of reporting the $1,500 he has received as expense allowance, he will attach to his return a certified copy of the document which authorized the municipality to pay him the $1,500.
There are always difficulties, but surely in this instance they are not insurmountable. This is a relieving clause so that all the elected representatives of the people in Canada will be placed on the same basis, and I am much surprised that there should be criticism of it.
It is not a relieving clause at all, the way the parliamentary assistant explained it. It is an encouragement to dishonesty.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: No.
That is exactly what it is.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: I will not enter into that field of discussion. I will not accuse any mayor or councillor of dishonesty.

All people in this country are human beings. If the parliamentary assistant is going to write into the Income Tax Act a provision that enables a city council or a municipal council to say, "We are going to authorize an addition of $1,500 a year"-

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: That is, if he already gets $3,000.

That is not relieving him of any tax on the $3,000. It merely means that the council has to pass an additional minute authorizing an additional $1,500 which the town will spend, and for which he will give the department an itemized account and receipts. He will have to do that.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: No.

It is still wide open, then, to all kinds of manipulation. You are not relieving him of anything on his $3,000 income. You are merely asking that town to set up another iniquitous minute which provides a loophole for anyone who wishes to take advantage of it to get a $1,500 offset from his taxes.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: I shall try to convince my hon. friend, then. We do not force the municipality to vote another $1,500. After all, these people are elected, and if the electors are not satisfied they will throw them out. In order to have its mayor benefit under this resolution, the municipality does not have to add $1,500. It just passes a new bylaw which will say, "From now on the mayor will receive $3,000 as indemnity and $1,500 as an expense allowance." And that will be all.
That sounds better.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Both can be done. I do not want to put ideas into the heads of municipal councils. But they are elected; they are responsible to their electors, and they can pay their mayor whatever indemnity or salary they wish.
Can they make it retroactive for six years?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: No, they cannot. I explained, in answer to the hon. member for Hamilton West (Mrs. Fairclough), that they can claim an exemption if it was paid to them as an expense allowance under these conditions. They will be exempt from the moment they pass a new bylaw or resolution.
But can a municipality pass a bylaw making it retroactive to 1946?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
They can do it; but it will not be allowed.
Income Tax Act

I must say I am a little confused. A couple of days ago the reeve of Burnaby wrote me a letter in which he said, "Kindly explain this new regulation." I have come here this afternoon to find out so that I can, in my own way, treat his inquiry with a certain amount of intelligence.
Because he has written me this letter, I can talk about his salary. He gets $6,000 a year, and a car is provided for him. I might say that we have a big municipality. As I understand it-and the parliamentary assistant will correct me if I am wrong-the council of the municipality of Burnaby can say, in their good judgment, "All right; our reeve is getting $6,000 a year. We have decided among ourselves"-whether the decision is made in council chamber or somewhere else-"that his expenses are $3,000 a year". That is 50 per cent.
I can be wrong in my understanding, but I am addressing this to the parliamentary assistant. Then the Burnaby municipal council, according to what I have heard this afternoon, can say to the reeve, "Your expenses are considered by this council for the year 1953 to be $3,000". That would not be right. The council might have a different opinion. They might consider his expenses to be higher than I do. Nevertheless they have that right.
When I answer the reeve, which I shall do in the next two or three days, when I get these facts clear, with my limited mental power, can I tell him that the council, in their own good judgment, can allow the reeve of Burnaby $3,000 for expenses on a $6,000 indemnity?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: If the council decides to vote for him an additional $3,000, it will be deductible. But if they want to vote for him an allowance of $3,000 out of the $6,000, not more than $2,000 will be deductible. He will be in the same position as my hon. friend, with his indemnity of $4,000 and his expense allowance of $2,000. I hope it is clear in my hon. friend's mind now.

It is not. May I say to the parliamentary assistant through you, Mr. Chairman, that it will be most difficult to get a member of parliament to come from Burnaby to this House of Commons. They will all be running for the reeveship.
Will this provision be wide enough to cover members of school boards and parks boards?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
No, it covers only elected representatives. The expression used is, "elected members of the governing bodies of incorporated municipalities".

Income Tax Act
That would include school boards.
Surely school boards and parks boards would be included in "governing bodies"?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: They are not governing bodies of incorporated municipalities; they are governing bodies of school communities.

To pursue that question further -because I, too, am interested in it-the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra and I know something about school boards in British Columbia. I expect he has served on them, and I certainly have. School boards in British Columbia are allowed only those expenses voted by themselves, and the expenses are very small. A school trustee is out of pocket to the extent of $400 or $500 a year in a large municipality. Are we not going to allow anything for them at all, when we allow the reeve $3,000 a year?

I do suggest some further consideration should be given to that point. The ordinary person reading this resolution would consider a school board or a parks board as coming within the meaning of "governing bodies". I do not see why they should not be entitled to exemption, as well as members of a council.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: I do not know of any member of a school board in my constituency who receives remuneration. It was not intended to cover school boards but only municipal councils.

I should like to raise my voice in support of the representations made by the last two speakers. This matter has been brought to my attention by members of school boards in my constituency who feel that they should receive similar exemption to that being granted to members of municipal councils.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Do they receive salaries?
Yes. I should like this matter to be considered further by the department.

If I understand the explanation aright, you are going to have a whole lot of trouble with members of school boards. In my province the meetings sometimes last for two or three days, and many of the members must travel considerable distances. We have anywhere from 70 to 90 small school units embodied in one large unit, and those men are certainly entitled to some exemption in connection with their expense accounts.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Consideration will be given to the representations made by the various hon. members who have spoken.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: Resolution agreed to.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I was going to suggest that perhaps resolutions Nos. 9 to 13 inclusive be taken together because they all deal with the exploration for petroleum and natural gas and mining development.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: I agree.
Agreed.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: I will ask the Minister of National Revenue to move an amendment to paragraph No. 11.

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue
speechtext:
I move:
That paragraph 11 of the proposed resolution to amend the Income Tax Act be amended by inserting therein immediately after the figures 1953, the word and figures "and 1954''.

I should like to commend the government upon its decision to encourage the drilling for oil and natural gas and also the development of mining properties. In my community there are probably 20 drilling operations going on at this time within a short distance of my own home. I understand that the program for the year ahead calls for the drilling of 154 wells north of the Peace river within British Columbia. A large field of natural gas has been brought into being, and oil has been discovered on a commercial scale within British Columbia. A great investment is required, and very often a well proves unprofitable. Under these clauses the operator will be given some encouragement to go on.
Mining is also carried on extensively in the Cariboo country. For every new mine that is brought into being in British Columbia there are probably 50 prospects which are explored and then abandoned. Large sums of money are spent on the development of these unprofitable prospects in the payment of wages, the purchase of supplies and equipment, and the building of roads and trails. It is a step in the right direction to encourage these mining and oil corporations and others in the work they are doing.
Pacific Petroleum will spend in the neighbourhood of $1 million per month right around Fort St. John in the Peace river country during the coming summer. Some of these wells will cost $750,000 or even more. It takes a very courageous man to stand at the edge of a hole that has been drilled a mile into the ground at tremendous cost and realize that it is totally unprofitable-and carry on. If this government wants to continue prosperity in Canada it should encourage in this way the investment of capital in mining and oil development, as well as in the development of other natural resources which in my part of the country are almost inexhaustible.

Except for the change in the date, I gather that resolution 11 is the same

as the resolution that has been in force for the last two years?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Exactly. Through an oversight the word and figures "and 1954" were omitted.
That is understandable. The only other suggestion I have to make would be to increase the period beyond what it is.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: It is three years.

I would like to have seen it increased to five years. Mapping out any exploration is a long-term project, and there are many programs involving $10 million or $20 million to be expended on exploration over a five or ten-year period. It is pretty obvious that these five resolutions are a definite part of a national policy for any Canadian government, but it would be of greater assistance if the period was increased to five years.
The only other suggestion I have to make in connection with income tax and to encourage the investment of capital in mining and the development of oil is that the depreciation allowance to shareholders be restored to the 30 per cent which was in effect prior to the war. Otherwise I think these five resolutions are satisfactory.

I should like to raise a point connected with these resolutions which was raised two years ago by the hon. member for Comox-Alberni, who I am sorry to see is not in his seat. At that time it was discussed by him and the minister. I should like to read briefly from the remarks made at that time by the hon. member for Comox-Alberni as well as from the remarks of the Minister of Finance. During the course of my remarks I shall point out that at that time the Minister of Finance said he understood that the Minister of Resources and Development would be discussing the matter. I have been in touch with the minister and he tells me that he has discussed the matter.
At page 3177 of Hansard for May 18, 1951, the hon. member for Comox-Alberni said:
It is a rather curious thing that the only natural resources receiving exemptions are oil, gas or mining and exploring for minerals. These commodities, of course, produce a great deal less revenue than the most important thing we have in Canada, our forest resources.
Then I skip to page 3178 and continue:
The way the matter stands now, a taxpayer can deduct his expenses so far as forestry and silviculture are concerned on the particular piece of property from which he is taking logs at the present time. No incentive at all is given to any of our great forestry corporations, large or small, to try to provide a supply of wood for the future. As a matter of fact, the government seems to have a negative approach to the whole question. They
Income Tax Act
say, "Yes, we realize it is a desirable thing that forests be put on a sustained yield basis". But on the other hand, they do not give any encouragement at all to people to invest money in growing trees. I am wondering whether there is any possibility of the minister giving some definite consideration to this problem within the next year, with a view to encouraging people to invest their money in growing timber.
Actually, the government seems to feel that someone might make a capital profit out of growing trees. It is that negative approach that annoys me. The minister will say: It is desirable to grow trees; on the other hand, if we encourage anyone to grow trees he may make a capital profit and I would not get anything out of it.
I believe that is a negative approach to the matter. I think something should be done to encourage people to invest their money in the future timber of this country. We allow people to lay up treasure in heaven by permitting them to deduct their charitable donations up to 10 per cent.
The minister and the hon. member for Comox-Alberni discussed treasure in heaven for a moment or two; then they came back to earth again and the minister said:
I do not know this of my own personal knowledge, Mr. Chairman,-

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: I do not like to raise a point of order. I did not come here briefed to discuss forestry or what should be done for the forest industry, but might I mention-
Is this a question of privilege?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: A point of order.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: A point of order. I want to inform my hon. friend that in the last four or five months forest management has been licensed on a sustained yield basis. The cost of acquiring licences is a capital cost, and the cost of maintaining sustained yield is allowed as an expense against income. This arrangement is satisfactory to the industry. The matter has been settled since the debate to which my hon. friend has referred, but the whole thing is out of order anyway.

Mr. Chairman, I had a slight suspicion that the parliamentary assistant might rise on a point of order, and I began by pointing out that there was a good precedent for this discussion, that this exact course was allowed two years ago. Incidentally, I am nearly through, but I should like to be allowed to finish my case. Actually I was about to read what was said with respect to the Minister of Resources and Development.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: All right.

The Minister of Finance said:
I do not know this of my own personal knowledge, Mr. Chairman, but I understand my colleague the Minister of Resources and Development is discussing the question which the hon. member for Comox-Alberni has raised, not only with the provinces but with an interdepartmental committee he has formed in his department.

Income Tax Act
The parliamentary assistant has indicated -and I am aware of it-that certain steps have been taken in the last two years. The Minister of Resources and Development informs me there is an arrangement with some of the provinces to stimulate reforestation under an agreement whereby the federal government will pay 20 per cent of the cost of reforestation of crown lands. That of course is something very different from the point raised by the hon. member for Comox-Alberni. Further, the Minister of Resources and Development has pointed out that there are other tax allowances made.
It is unfortunate that the hon. member for Comox-Alberni is not here, because he has an intimate knowledge of the industry which I do not possess. I have raised this matter because it was raised and considered two years ago, at which time the minister indicated that he was interested in it and would pursue it further. It seems to me not irrelevant to find out exactly what has happened. I hope there are others here at the present time who may know more about the actual facts than I do. It seems to me it is an important matter and it should not take much time; so I hope, Mr. Chairman, that you will allow the debate to continue.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: On that point, the only thing I can say is that I am informed that discussions with the industry have taken place and that the industry is reasonably satisfied with the arrangements that have been made.
I believe that is not the case with British Columbia.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: I did not come briefed to discuss reforestation. The industry mentioned has nothing to do with the resolution we are studying now. If hon. members want to raise the question on the bill when the minister is here, I am sure he will be delighted to deal with it, but this matter is not included in the resolution and I am not prepared to discuss it. I have given the only information I have, namely that there was an understanding with the industry and that it is working satisfactorily. Beyond that I cannot go, and since the discussion is out of order I do not feel that it should be allowed to continue.

We should not be prevented from making our submissions, because it is our hope that the question will be given further consideration and that some steps will be taken to meet the difficulty by means of legislation. After all, these resolutions are designed to aid in the development of our Canadian resources. The development of our forest resources is in exactly the same category, and we are merely asking that steps
[Mr. Macdonnell (Greenwood) J
should be taken to help further the development of that great natural resource. The parliamentary assistant has gone so far as to claim that the problem has already been met.

speechtext: I said I was informed.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, at the time this debate was adjourned I was making a few observations on the resolution to set up the committee. I have no desire to delay the setting up of that committee, but I was pointing out that I thought the policy pursued by the government so far, in setting up the C.B.C. as a regulatory body to allocate the air waves, was the proper kind of development for a country like Canada. The proposal by the government that television should be handled in the same way is, in my opinion, absolutely sound. The principle has already been proven in the case of Trans-Canada Air Lines, for example, where the government undertook to retain under their control the main airways, and where they established cross-country air lines and basic air lines with a proper organization. Trans-Canada Air Lines has proven one of the most effective and one of the safest air lines in the world.
Despite the fact that the Canadian Pacific Railway is used as the yardstick, I think the Canadian National Railways is a sound development even though they have had some handicap in their operations, particularly in respect of financing. As members of parliament, we will next week have the right to examine the operations of the Canadian National Railways and then be in a position to assure the Canadian people that the railway is not only sound financially but is doing a reasonably good job for the people of Canada.
Canadian Arsenals Limited is another example of what is proposed now for television. That corporation is the basis for the munitions industry and they too are pioneering, setting a pattern and developing regulations that should guide private industry. If we are to judge by international tensions at the present time the munitions industry is going to be a very important industry
3150	HOUSE OF
Special Committee on Broadcasting in the future. I am only sorry the government did not follow through in the case of pipe lines, where they have farmed out the natural resources without retaining the main lines as common carriers. I think they departed from their policy there, but they may get back to it later.
With respect to television there was the accusation the other night, and I heard it from several members of the house, that it added up to a straight monopoly. Well, we certainly have not had a monopoly in the case of radio broadcasting. The Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Drew) dispelled that illusion a few nights ago when he put on record the fact that on the trans-Canada network which the C.B.C. operates at the present time there are only 10 C.B.C. stations and there are 17 privately operated stations. On the dominion network the hon. gentleman pointed out that there are 26 privately-owned stations as against one C.B.C. station. In the whole field, on both networks at the present time you have 36 private stations as opposed to 18 C.B.C. stations.
I think those figures, put on the record by the Leader of the Opposition, proved pretty conclusively that there is no such thing as a monopoly being developed there. It is the other way around. The C.B.C. has only half of the total number of stations on both networks. The charge of monopoly, or potential monopoly, in so far as radio is concerned, does not hold true. It adds up to the fact that somebody has not thought the problem through or checked the facts very carefully.
I think the government's policy of retaining the main television stations in this country is a sound one. If we establish television stations in Toronto, Montreal, Ottawa, Halifax, Vancouver, Winnipeg and Calgary, being the main projected stations, in my opinion that will be sound. It is only reasonable to suppose that the basic stations in this country will be built in large centres of population, though I am not unmindful of the fact that there is a broad field for private operators, just as there was in the development of radio. I do not suppose, for example, that Newfoundland will get television for a long time. I think that in that end of the country television will develop as the C.B.C. did. For example, in Cape Breton and in Newfoundland we had private stations for 20 years before the C.B.C. came into that area.
The proposal to establish a main station at Halifax, which is 360 miles west of Cape Breton island-and Newfoundland is about 90 miles further-is going to have the result of delaying television in that part of the country for a long time unless the private operators enter the picture in those sparsely


settled sections. The servicing of those areas is not economic at this time under the regulations laid down for the setting up of the basic stations. I was glad to hear the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. McCann) or the Minister of Transport (Mr. Chevrier), I am not sure which, announce that an application for a private station had been made by CJCB at Sydney. This station will develop television in that part of the country. I believe that station will be well equipped, perhaps as well equipped as the C.B.C. stations. In that way Newfoundland might get television across the 90 miles of water from Sydney.
I assume that some private stations will be established in the area between Halifax and Sydney to carry the regular programs from the main station at Halifax to Sydney and across to Newfoundland and Prince Edward Island. I believe the attitude that the whole development should be exclusively in the hands of the C.B.C. and under government control is unrealistic when you think of the great spaces and concentration of population that you have in the centres where the government is establishing stations at this time. Someone has to serve the outlying sections. If the pattern developed by the C.B.C. in connection with radio, which I think was a very realistic one, is followed in television there is some assurance that while the government is doing the job in the main centres, the private stations will be doing the same kind of job in the fields that are less lucrative at this time.
There is just one observation I should like to make now, and that concerns the 15 per cent that is being charged on television receiving sets to replace the old radio licence fee. I am thinking now of the sections that will be developed by the private stations. I feel that it is unreasonable to put a 15 per cent tax on television sets in those areas which are not going to be served by the C.B.C., because the private stations will not receive any benefit from that.

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue
subsubtopic: APPOINTMENT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext: The C.B.C. will be supplying programs to all those private stations.

subsubtopic: APPOINTMENT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext:
I hope they will; but as I pointed out a moment ago the distances in my own section-I took that as an example because I am familiar with the geography there-will cause long delays before Halifax will be able to send programs through to Cape Breton, 360 miles away. There will be a period of some years during which we are going to have to pay a tax of 15 per cent on television sets, and that revenue will go to the organization that does not give us any service. That is something that can be considered, and perhaps some modification can

be made by way of exempting areas which do not receive any service from this organization.
Now, Mr. Speaker, that is about all I want to say. With reference to C.B.C. policy, I want to say that while I agree with what they are doing, and the job they are doing in developing radio as well as the job I expect they will do in developing television, there is one part of their policy that can be criticized. When the Canadian Congress of Labour visited the cabinet here on March 6 they made strong representations concerning the C.B.C.'s approach to labour relations. When a number of the C.B.C. employees were seeking, through legitimate channels, the right of collective bargaining as set down in the national labour code, there was some intimidation and interference by management.
I think that is a bad policy for an organization that has to come to the government for appropriations, and which depends upon the taxpayers for financing. It should have the good will of all members in this house. It is not a big problem. I believe government or crown companies should be the first to show the way to the average industrialist who may be a bit selfish. I think it is a bad policy for the C.B.C. to do anything in a public way that would cause the Canadian Congress of Labour to offer criticism on the matter of their labour relations.
The hon. member for Moose Jaw (Mr. Thatcher) made a very heated appeal to the government for the establishment of a television station in Saskatchewan. He pointed out that that province, jammed in between Manitoba and Alberta, would not get a basic television station. I know that results in discrimination in many ways. If there were a basic station established immediately in each province, it would create a demand for television sets. You see, the merchant in Saskatchewan is being discriminated against in that he cannot sell television sets because there will be no television. I think he had a legitimate complaint, because all the television sets will be sold in Alberta and Manitoba.
While the hon. member was speaking, it struck me that perhaps the province of Saskatchewan may do something about that. There is a government in power in that province which believes in the policies laid down by the C.B.C., and there is no doubt in my mind but that they would go along with the policy now being pursued with regard to television. If this government cannot see its way clear to establishing a station in Regina, Prince Albert or some other central spot, could the provincial government of Saskatchewan obtain a franchise to set up a station

Special Committee on Broadcasting and operate it? Perhaps that is a way out. It would remove the discrimination against the merchants in the matter of selling television sets, at a time when there is going to be an increased demand for television sets in other provinces in this country.

I wish to say a few words about this resolution. I was prepared to add something to the debate last Wednesday, when I intended to make some extended remarks. I know the government is in a hurry to establish this committee, so I shall be rather brief today.
This important resolution should have been proceeded with two months ago, when it came up on January 27. Then it was sidetracked until March 17. Even at that date I am sure it would have gone through in a very short time had it not been for the speech of the Minister of Transport. I am sorry he is not present today. He carried the question so far afield when he spoke on behalf of the government that it looked like a real red-hot political appeal and campaign propaganda. That speech on that occasion aroused such antagonism across the house and all sides that the debate continued, and that is the reason why the passing of this resolution has been delayed and the committee has not been set up. That delay in the setting up of the committee is wholly accounted for by the actions of the government itself.
When I rose the other night to make a few remarks someone called out: "Why cause a delay?" Before I make my main remarks may I say that there is no delay caused by the opposition. The whole delay in the setting up of this committee rests entirely upon the government itself.

I want to refer to a few of the remarks that the Minister of Transport made. He started out with a very fine lecture on how the union of Canada was obtained. He took first of all the building of the Canadian Pacific Railway. I intended to elaborate on

Special Committee on Broadcasting this, as he has done, by referring to history, but I am not going to subject the house to these long remarks. However, I do wish to make a few remarks on one of the points that the minister mentioned, namely, the building of the Canadian Pacific Railway. If the real history of that project is looked into carefully it will be found that credit for it must go to some far-seeing men of British Columbia. That great railway was to link the Atlantic with the Pacific. There was considerable opposition to it. Several reasons were advanced why the railway could not be built on Canadian soil from coast to coast. When British Columbia learned this they had not completed their contract of union with the Dominion of Canada, and they said: "We will not complete our contract until the Canadian Pacific Railway is built, and built on Canadian soil to reach Vancouver." Instead of making a detour through the United States to get into Vancouver the road was built on allCanadian soil. Therefore I say that the far-seeing minds of some of the people of British Columbia of that time deserve all the credit, instead of giving it to anyone else, for the building of the Canadian Pacific Railway on all-Canadian soil through to Vancouver.
I will not deal with other matters taken up by the Minister of Transport but I shall mention one point that he dealt with with regard to union. It was very pleasant to me and I am sure to others to hear mention made of a number of outstanding Canadians who had a great deal to do with issues leading up to radio and television. The Minister of Transport referred to some of them while he was speaking, and as he always does, he said they belonged to the Tory party. He also used the words "Conservative party". I was very glad to hear the names of such men as Sir John A. Macdonald, the Right Hon. Arthur Meighen, Viscount R. B. Bennett and Sir R. L. Borden. He could have gone a little farther and mentioned some other names in this connection, but their names have been left off Hansard and perhaps I shall leave them to their record.
I listened to and afterwards read the speech of the Minister of Transport, and I must say this: If that speech was the voice of the government, all I can say is that I cannot realize that the Liberal party has sunk so low in its political propaganda as to acknowledge it as being the voice of the Liberal party. Some of the remarks were admirably described by the hon. member for Eglinton (Mr. Fleming) in his speech of March 17, as reported at page 3013 of Hansard, when he said:
That is the most shocking kind of demagogic claptrap.
[Mr. McLure.l
I wish the minister were here. It is unfortunate that a speech of that kind should be made just at the time when we are nearing an election, because it brings up a racial issue that is not so evident as one would think on reading the speech of the hon. gentleman. However, that is all I will say with regard to this at the present time.

I am glad he came in. The unfortunate part of this debate is the very strong words that have been used against private interests. That is something that should be dealt with by someone. In our province of Prince Edward Island we have a number of private enterprises that are good concerns. We have three outstanding ones, namely, the Maritime Central Airways, the CFCY Radio Company, and, in the field of transportation again, the Northumberland Ferries Limited. In some of the speeches made with reference to private enterprise very strong remarks were made. I understood the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) to say that the business activities of the Canadian Association of Broadcasters were subversive of the interests of the Canadian nation. The hon. member for Spa-dina (Mr. Croll), as reported at page 3021 of Hansard, and speaking in support of the government, said, with respect to the observations of the hon, member for Rosetown-Biggar:
In the main I share his views, and I hope they will prevail.
This condemnation of private enterprise in radio has brought forth protests. Members are receiving them every day-protests saying that those who are operating private radio broadcasting stations have been slandered by the speeches made in this debate.
And this brings me to the situation in respect of radio in my own province. As hon. members know, we are served by radio station CFCY, which is known throughout Canada as the "Friendly Voice of the Mari-times". This radio station is one of the best examples to be found anywhere of true private enterprise and public service. It is owned and operated by the Island Radio Broadcasting Company. The station not only gives a service to Prince Edward Island, but also has the largest coverage in the maritime provinces of any radio station.
I would hope that those hon. members who have used such harsh language when refer-

ring to private enterprise in radio will be men enough either to withdraw or to modify their remarks at the earliest opportunity. Station CFCY has operated as an independent radio station for 33 years, and has given a first-class service not only to Prince Edward Island but to the maritime provinces. The company operating the station has developed some of its own programs, one of which, the Merry Islanders, will be known to many hon. members. This program, which is broadcast across Canada, has been the production of that private company; and it has several more to its credit.
During its 33 years of operation station CFCY has spent its own money. It has never received in all that time one single nickel from public funds. Right at this moment they are investigating and doing their own research work in regard to the television which undoubtedly will come to the maritime provinces, and to Prince Edward Island as well.
I have nothing further to say at this time.
I am pleased to see the Minister of Transport (Mr. Chevrier) back in his seat. As I said earlier, I thought his speech on March 17 -and I say this with the respect I always have for him-was one which I had not believed a man in his normal senses would make, and one which was most detrimental in times such as these, when across Canada we are trying to live in peace and harmony.
I thank the house for this opportunity to say a few words with respect to station CFCY.
