speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before the minister speaks I wish to correct two statements that have been made with respect to broadcasting. The first was made by the hon. member for York South (Mr. Noseworthy) when he said that private stations would not give time for the expression of opinions which were not their own or, presumably, not those of capital.
Let me say this, that if there was one station that gave time to the communist party in this country, it was station CKEY in Toronto owned by Jack Kent Cooke, who owns newspapers and a baseball team, who is certainly a capitalist, and one whose opinions would be farther from the ideologies of the Labour-Progressive party than any other man I can think of in Canada. Yet he considered it a public service to allow them to use his radio station.
I understand that, because of the many complaints about his allowing the vehicle of his radio station to be used by interests with which he so violently disagreed, they have now been stopped from broadcasting. But that is only because of the protests that were received. When anybody says that a private station will not be host to opinions
3154	HOUSE OF
Special Committee on Broadcasting which are not their own, I give him the direct lie and say that that is not so.
The Minister of Transport (Mr. Chevrier) gave an exhibition of a well-fed sea gull flying away when he spoke last St. Patrick's day on the question of radio. His remarks have been dealt with adequately iby other speakers on this side and I shall not delay the house any further in that connection.
There is one thing in connection with television that I wish to bring to the attention of the house. In the Toronto area the great majority of television users are tuned in or videoed in, or whatever expression it is, to the Buffalo station. The area between Toronto and Hamilton is to be blocked out from receiving the Hamilton station because the C.B.C. Toronto station is to have .a monopoly. I disagree most strenuously with that policy. Incidentally, I do not have a television set, but I live in the area and I think this is just another example of the dictatorial methods adopted by the C.B.C. to make a competitive station beam its waves away from an area served by the C.B.C.
With regard to the policy of having only one station in the community, I understand that television channels, while more limited than radio channels, are able to extend only a short distance. A television station in one centre will not interfere with a television station in a centre 500 miles away. With a single television station in the Toronto area the people there will be precluded from viewing any other station but the United States stations. In other words, the people in Toronto who do not wish to view CBLT will be driven to viewing United States stations. I think that is faulty reasoning; I think that is faulty policy and I suggest it should be considered by the committee.
A number of universities in the United States have established television stations and they have been found to be of great value both to the university and to the community. Despite the fact that there may be stations owned by private companies or by the chains, the university stations have proved to be of great value. Should the University of Toronto wish to establish a television station it would be precluded from doing so under the regulations. I feel that that is a defect in the policy.
That is really all I wanted to say as I do not wish to hold up the debate any longer.

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue
subsubtopic: APPOINTMENT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext:
This has been a most interesting and informative discussion although it has taken longer than we anticipated. There may be some good reasons for that and I do not think that it has been time lost. My understanding of setting up a committee to do the work of parliament is that it will expedite the business of the house, but that has not proved to be so in this instance.
The discussion has ranged over a good deal of territory and has been participated in by members of all parties on all sides of the house. We know where we stand; we know where the different members of the different parties stand with respect to the C.B.C. and broadcasting in general. I am glad that that particular stand has been taken. If one were to attempt to answer all the matters which have been raised it would take much longer than the time I have at my disposal.
The hon. member for Eglinton (Mr. Fleming) was concerned about the fee for radio sets and the manner in which television was going to be financed. Those two matters were cleared up pretty well by the statement made by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) in his budget speech. Both these matters have given us considerable concern. The hon. member for Eglinton has brought them to the attention of the government on a number of occasions and we have had them in mind for this past year. As we were approaching the

end of March when licences were renewable, we considered that that would be the proper time to take this action.
I have pointed out on other occasions that the development of television in this country is very expensive. Although we have been criticized by the hon. member for Moose Jaw (Mr. Thatcher) for not going faster, I have no apology to make for having counselled the C.B.C. to go slowly in this development.
The excise tax on television receiving sets should help to finance this organization for the next few years. There are something like 200,000 sets now in Canada and even on a conservative estimate it is expected that the payment of excise taxes over the next few years at the rate of 15 per cent on the sets to be produced will bring in considerable revenue. At this time at least the average television set costs about $200 in the manufacturer's hands. Fifteen per cent of that is $30. I am told by people in the electronics industry that a set will use one tube a year. These tubes cost approximately $63 and the tax on that will be fifteen times six or approximately another $9. Therefore all told, when a person starts out and wants to be a television viewer, he will contribute to the national treasury something like $39 or $40.
I have figured out that that is equivalent to paying a licence fee of $15 in advance for two and a half or three years. Therefore I think that answers the question of the hon. member for Eglinton.
The hon. member for Cape Breton South (Mr. Gillis) referred to his own particular community when he expressed doubt about the fairness of the excise tax being payable on receiving sets that would be used in his community because of the fact that he thought that the people there would have no C.B.C. service. They will have C.B.C. service because part of the program is that by recordings what we call sustaining programs will go to the private stations. He took it for granted that there would be a private station in that locality.
With reference to the hon. member who has just spoken about the policy in Saskatchewan, that is a matter concerning which I am not prepared to give him a definite answer at the moment, but it can be brought up in the committee when the officials of the corporation will be present and I am sure they will give him the correct answer.
I was particularly interested in the speech made by the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Drew). He went back a long way and quoted in part from Hansard of May 18, 1932, at which time the Hon. Mr. Bennett, then prime minister, moved second reading of

Special Committee on Broadcasting Bill 94 respecting radio broadcasting. Of course it is his right, if he so wishes, to quote whatever parts of a debate he chooses to quote, but I should like to point out that on that occasion, as found at page 3035 of Hansard, Mr. Bennett used these words:
Private ownership must necessarily discriminate between densely and sparsely populated areas.
I suggest to the Leader of the Opposition that he would have given a much clearer picture to the house of the history of the development of radio if he had gone back a little further in the debate, which I intend to do for the purpose of pointing out briefly the reasons that were given by Mr. Bennett for having the set-up that we have today. At page 3035 Mr. Bennett said:
First of all, this country must be assured of complete Canadian control of broadcasting from Canadian sources, free from foreign interference or influence.
That is exactly what we have been contending. Then he goes on to say:
But it seems to me clear-

I will deal with that later. Mr. Bennett went on to say:
But it seems to me clear that in Canada the system we can most profitably employ is one which, in operation and control, responds most directly to the popular will and the national need. In this stage of our national development we have problems peculiar to ourselves and we must reach a solution of them through the employment of all available means. The radio has a place in the solution of all those problems. It becomes, then, the duty of parliament to safeguard it in such a way that its fullest benefits may be assured to the people as a whole.
Then he goes on to give his second reason:
Secondly, no other scheme than that of public ownership can ensure to the people of this country, without regard to class or place, equal enjoyment of the benefits and pleasures of radio broadcasting.
Then he went on to say, as was quoted by the Leader of the Opposition:
Equality of service is assured by the plan which calls for a chain of high power stations throughout Canada. And furthermore, the particular requirements of any community may be met by the installation of low power stations by means of which local broadcasting service may be obtained.
That reason was definitely outlined at that time. Then he went on to give his third reason and said, as found at page 3036:
Then there is a third reason to which I might refer, and one which I believe must commend itself to every hon. member in this chamber. The use of the air, or the air itself, whatever you may please to call it, that lies over the soil or land of Canada is a natural resource over which we have complete jurisdiction under the recent decision of the privy council. I believe that there is no government in Canada that does not regret today that

Special Committee on Broadcasting it has parted with some of these natural resources for considerations wholly inadequate and on terms that do not reflect the principle under which the crown holds the natural resources in trust for all the people. In view of these circumstances and of the further fact that broadcasting is a science that is only yet in its infancy and about which we know little yet, I cannot think that any government would be warranted in leaving the air to private exploitation and not reserving it for development for the use of the people ... I think, Mr. Speaker, that that is a third and adequate reason why we should proceed with the bill.
I think it might be interesting to the house to get a little bit of the background. In 1928 the Aird commission was set up and they laid down the principles on which policies could be made by any government thereafter with reference to radio broadcasting. They made their report on the 11th of September, 1929, to the Hon. Mr. Cardin, who was then minister of transport. Let us recall what took place. The report was presented. In 1930 the parliament was dissolved, an election was held, and Mr. Bennett came into power. It was not until two years later that he implemented the recommendations of the Aird report and set up the Canadian radio broadcasting commission. At that time the recommendations of the Aird commission report were followed. Yet we on this side of the house are criticized because we have followed the recommendations of the Massey commission, which presented its report not very long ago.
After Mr. Bennett had finished his speech in 1932 Mr. Lapointe spoke, and I want to quote part of what he said to show the consistency of the position of the Liberal party. On that occasion he said, as found at page 3036 of Hansard for May 18:
I just wish to endorse the views expressed by my right hon. friend the Prime Minister and to say that I am in full accord with the principle embodied in this bill. I have been supporting this principle from the first, more particularly after the work of the Aird commission, but I knew the difficulties in the way and the strength of the propaganda carried on to prevent the work of that commission from having the results which we witness today.
I am pleased with the work which was done by the committee which has been studying this question, and I congratulate the members of that committee on the excellent work which they did. I congratulate the house upon having this bill introduced at the present session, and I congratulate the people of Canada on the principle which is represented in the bill.
The leader of the C.C.F. party at that time, Mr. Woodsworth, said, as found at page 3037 of Hansard for the same date:
I should like to associate myself with the last speaker in congratulating the Prime Minister on his promptness in bringing down this bill to implement the report which has been unanimously adopted. May I further express my own very great appreciation of the admirable statement which the Prime Minister has made.


I quote these remarks, Mr. Speaker, to indicate that the Liberal party and the C.C.F. party have consistently supported the policies and the principles that were laid down at that time, and do so today. What has been the policy of the Tory party in the last fifteen or sixteen years? Under Manion, under Hanson, under the hon. member for Peel (Mr. Graydon), under Bracken and under the present Leader of the Opposition they have vacillated from year to year. The other day in the speech which the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Drew) made, he wants to get back on the bandwagon-because he believes in public support in this country for the publicly-owned, publicly-operated and publicly-controlled broadcasting system; but he is only half-way on the bandwagon, hanging on. He is for public support of radio broadcasting but not for public support of television. That is the stand which he has taken. He wants to run with the hare and hunt with the hounds.
Until he spoke on March 18 we had not had an open declaration of the policy of the Conservative party in reference to this great public utility.
I am not going to take time to go as deeply into this as I might, but I want to put on the record part of an editorial which appeared in the Ottawa Journal, which cannot by any stretch of the imagination be considered a paper which is favourable to the Liberal party. It has been the chief standby of the Conservative party in this district during my lifetime. Here is an editorial which should open the eyes of the leader of the Tory party. It is headed "No private rights to the air".
The Journal always has taken the position that there must be strict control by the public, which of course means control by an agency of the dominion government, over radio broadcasting in Canada. Exactly the same arguments apply-more so indeed-in the case of television.
The Journal believes it would be a grave blunder, and in fact irretrievable, to let TV escape into private hands for private exploitation and private profit.
The Minister of Transport (Mr. Chevrier)- ... in the Commons, spoke of Canada's traditional policy in radio matters as "based on the coordinated efforts of public and private enterprise", and to that statement we take no exception. But the private element in the effort must not be permitted to acquire any inalienable right to use of the air channels and the air waves for its own purposes-there must be always the overriding authority of the public interest.
In the field of radio broadcasting there are large numbers of stations privately owned and operated, but they are subject to general regulation by the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation and they cannot acquire, by usage or use, any vested right to a place in the air. That is as it should be. It is only by constant vigilance, and resistance to the plausible importunities of private broadcasting

interests, that this position has been maintained. Time after time the Canadian Association of Broadcasters has returned to the assault, bent on depriving C.B.C. of its statutory rights-always so far it has been defeated. They have in recent years been demanding television rights.
Television today, at least in Canada, is in the stage of trial and experiment, and nobody knows quite what it will become. Already millions of dollars of the taxpayers' money have been spent, and many more millions will go into the enterprise before it is established on any secure and national basis.
Enthusiasts contend that TV will revolutionize our way of life, and change our social picture as drastically as the automobile has altered it. Others recall that a few years ago just such things were being said about radio-and that nothing much has happened. It is clear, however, between these conflicting views, that television must be developed in this country with care and restraint, taking advantage of such lessons as we can learn from TV in Britain and the United States, taking the best of both systems and avoiding, if we can, the worst features of both.
Our task will be simplified if we refuse flatly to let private interests get a foot in the television door-especially at this stage. A time may come, the uncertainties of today reduced, and a fluid situation become stable, when we shall want to see TV shared between public and private stations -as radio is shared-but always with public control beyond question. That time is not yet visible. But today and always, in television as in radio, the public interest must be the governing factor.
I could go -on, Mr. Speaker, and give lots of press notices and lots of public opinion with reference to how the C.B.C. should be handled. This is an important transitional point in the development of both sound broadcasting and television, but more particularly the latter.
I infer from the speech of the Leader of the Opposition that he makes this more or less a political issue. We welcome it as a political issue because we know where the public of this country stands. When he is talking for private interests in television, what does he in effect say? He says that the few hundred who wish to engage in television shall get into the cities and get the commercial advertising and have the gravy; and you, the rest of Canada, the 99 per cent, shall pay the shot.
That is his policy and if he wants to make that a political issue in the not too far distant future-well, he had better review it, because I am sure that the heat of the summer is going to sweat a lot of the water out of that particular policy.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have not before taken part in any discussion of a pipe-line bill because I considered it purely a matter concerning the west or, at any rate, a matter on which I was not familiar or competent to speak. However, the question of pipe lines has now become one which has a tremendous effect on the whole Canadian economy. As one who is interested in mining I do not feel that I can allow this bill to pass without saying something about it.
The Canadian economy is divided geographically by three main north and south barriers. One is in the maritimes, roughly New Brunswick and the Gaspe peninsula, which separate Nova Scotia from the industrial lower St. Lawrence and Montreal. The next is the great Canadian shield which comes down on the barren shores of lake Superior and which, up to now, has been one of the great obstacles of trade between the east and west of Canada. It is nearly 1,000 miles across and its potential wealth is only just now being understood. The third north and south barrier is, of course, the Rocky mountains.
The first barrier is being filled in by the new ore discoveries in New Brunswick and the very large copper deposits on the Gaspe peninsula. The Rocky mountains are also benefiting by a tremendous boom in Alberta and, despite the physical obstacle, their terror is being lessened. Northern Ontario, with its small settlements, still remains the major gulf separating the east and the west. It is an area about which we have a primary duty to do something.
Now, this barrier is, we think and we hope, minerally rich but deficient in fuel. I want to say something in this connection about electricity and gas. While electricity is

' Mid-Continent Pipelines Limited a primary source of power it is not, except in special circumstances, an economic source of heat because it is more useful as a source of power. Canada has a policy with regard to the export of electricity. Electricity has only been exported under licence, and great restrictions have been imposed upon its exportation. I think that is wise, because once electricity is exported and the continuous flow of electricity across an international border has been established it is almost impossible to stop it. The experience of the Hydro Electric Power Commission of Ontario is a case in point.
I feel that if we once export natural gas we may find that natural gas would suffer a fate similar to that of electricity. In other words, dependent industries will be built up, and it will be impossible to stop the flow of gas once export has been started. I would, therefore, certainly be very careful in granting any right to export natural gas. There may be special circumstances. There may be areas which are gas deficient, and it may be possible to work out a quid pro quo with the United States. However, our dealings in this regard have not been very successful in the past. Consequently I would hesitate to approve any bill which sought the exportation of natural gas when we have an area in northern Ontario which is so deficient in fuel.
The situation in the northern United States-I am a small shareholder in a gas utility company operating in the United States and this is what the directors say-is one in which they look forward to a tremendous expansion in the development of industry through the enlargement of the natural gas flow from Texas and the midcontinent field. If we export our gas into this market, surely they are going to increase their industries and their economy through the use of what must be, in my opinion, a basic Canadian raw material. I know that is so from the reports I get from companies in which I have a small interest. Let us, therefore, be very careful about what we do with this asset.
It has been said that it will be more expensive to send gas across northern Ontario than it would be if we could possibly work out a quid pro quo with the United States. In my opinion, Mr. Speaker, the working out of any agreement such as that with the United States is virtually an impossibility. We have spent nearly 50 years trying to work out an agreement with regard to the St. Lawrence deep waterway. Are we any more likely to work out an agreement on a basic matter of energy, and do we expect that we could do it in a short period of

time? I do not believe that this house would be justified in thinking that we could.
I come now to the potentialities of northern Ontario. I have said that northern Ontario remains the great barrier, and the desolation of northern Ontario is the great geographical barrier to our whole national development. To what can we look forward in northern Ontario? Today it is virtually a wilderness, but it is a wilderness largely because it is deficient in fuel. Mineral deposits have been discovered, and one was discovered just a month or so ago at a place called Emo which is about 20 miles west of Fort Frances. This is right in the area where the development of minerals is needed. This is a nickel and possibly copper- although that I do not know-deposit. So far big widths of sulphides have been discovered. Over 10 feet of massive pyrrhotite was found in one drill hole. May I say that sulphides are the host ore of both nickel and copper. The companies interested are the major companies in Canada, Noranda, Falconbridge, Ventures, Prospectors, Airways and many others.
Now, Mr. Speaker, the development of sulphide ore can be attained with the use of natural gas in the smelting operation. It is most important that if we are to develop an area such as Emo, which has only recently been discovered, there must be some form of cheap fuel and it must be there constantly and in great volume. I mention Emo just as an example of what can be done if we have cheap fuel in northwestern Ontario. Emo may remain a moose pasture or it may become a prosperous community. Natural gas could be the deciding factor.
I turn now to Steep Rock. Unfortunately, natural gas cannot be used, so far as I know, in steel making. Coke and coal are needed for the smelting of iron. A chemical process is one in which natural gas cannot do the essential job of reduction. It requires a carbon dioxide gas and some method by which the oxygen can be separated from the ore. I mention that because it is one of the great problems of research in this country to find out some way in which natural gas could be used in the steel process. As I say, I am not a steel man, and I am not a chemist, but it seems to me that is one of the problems on which a great deal of active research needs to be done.
I now come to Sudbury. Here the greatest benefit of all for mining is likely to take place. Nickel ore can be economically reduced by a process entailing the use of natural gas as a fuel, or at least that is the opinion of the experts of the Sherritt-Gordon mine and of the people who are

building the great petrochemical industry in Alberta, particularly at Fort Saskatchewan, who are going to use the Lynn Lake nickel ore for treatment by natural gas. The Sudbury basin, the north rim of which is just now coming into its own, has the possibility of adding to the known great mineral store; one of the great assets of the free world an unknown but incredible increase in ore reserves. Can we as Canadians do anything else except see that that natural Canadian fuel gets taken to this tremendous mineral storehouse? Even if it costs more to bring it there, Mr. Speaker, can we deny the development of this district the use of this natural fuel? In my opinion it would be almost treason to do so. Here again, as I have said, the chemical process, the reduction and leaching processes are new. The cost of reduction, the costs of bringing out the metal are not known, but the best opinion, the best engineering opinion and the best chemical opinion in Canada is that it will tremendously aid in the refining and production of nickel. In my opinion we cannot allow this fuel to bypass the Sudbury area.
I now come to Toronto. The Toronto market for gas at the present moment is comparatively small. It is small because of the high cost of gas made from coal, artificial gas. The cost of gas in Toronto to the consumer is, I understand, $1.60 per thousand cubic feet; but the other disadvantage is that artificial gas has a heating value of only 450 B.T.U.'s; whereas natural gas has a heating value of 1,000 B.T.U.'s. Natural gas could be brought to Toronto for approximately $1 per thousand cubic feet. The Toronto market, as I say, must be developed, and it can only be developed by natural gas. At the present time the Union Gas Company, and I gather one of the subsidiaries of the Imperial Oil, are providing Toronto with part of its gas; but the Union Gas Company has very limited or comparatively limited reserves. To build up the Toronto market by taking the Union Gas Company's reserves would be to deplete the assets of that company and would be an unfair thing to ask it to do. Therefore the gas market in Toronto cannot be built up unless there is a definite promise that an adequate supply of natural gas will be available to that metropolis. The only way that an adequate supply of natural gas can be made available to that city and the whole surrounding area is by an all-Canadian pipe line of quite considerable size running from the gas and oil fields of Saskatchewan and Alberta.
I want to emphasize one thing more about the Toronto market. When I say "the

Mid-Continent Pipelines Limited Toronto market" I mean the metropolitan market of Toronto, Hamilton and Oshawa, that whole industrial area. It is likely that once the St. Lawrence deep waterway is completed we can expect a population of five million people living in the industrial area between Oshawa and Hamilton, a distance of about 60 miles. I have never seen any place in the world where an industrial expansion looked so promising as it does in that area at the present time. The Delaware basin from the sea past Philadelphia to the new huge U.S. Steel mill at Trenton and the area around Toronto and Hamilton, if the latter is given cheap water transportation and cheap fuel, can duplicate each other in a comparatively few years. However, the Toronto market is just one.
It is essential that this gas, this national Canadian asset, must also be used by the province of Quebec, the metropolis of Montreal, and also, Mr. Speaker, by the base metal producers in that province who would also benefit, because of the fact that their sulphide ore can be treated by the use of natural gas for their smelting and refining processes. The problem is one which cannot wait much longer. We have the natural barrier of northern Ontario. We have to fill up that area; and the only way we can fill it up is by developing a large and prosperous mining industry. The potential has already been shown to us. We have the huge nickel belt at Sudbury crying out for an adequate supply of cheap fuel for smelting purposes. We have the Toronto-Hamilton-Oshawa market with a potential of some five million people waiting to develop their industries through the use of natural gas. We have the Quebec smelters, and we have the great port and metropolis of Montreal.
On the face of that can we, Mr. Speaker, countenance the export and the loss of this great natural asset? I do not think we can. And I would hope that the policy in developing or granting charters to pipe-line companies for the transmission of natural gas would be such that it would not grant permission for the export of gas.
I realize there are certain places in the United States that are gas-deficient and power-deficient-and I am thinking of parts of the state of Washington and of Oregon. I think, too, of the heavy water plant either in the state of Washington or in the state of Idaho, I am not sure which.
But that is not the problem which arises under this bill. As I said, it is a technical problem I am not fully competent to discuss. However, I do suggest to the house that, like electricity, natural gas belongs here to fuel

Mid-Continent Pipelines Limited the furnaces and provide the smelting facilities of our great base metals industry. It is needed to fill in the blanks on the map of Canada. It is needed in northern Ontario which some day, we hope, will be industrialized through the development of its mineral riches. It is needed for industrial use in the great and growing metropolises which, just as sure as night follows day, will come, once the St. Lawrence deep waterway is built, and our great lakes ports become tidewater ports.
I would be almost a traitor to this country if I did not see to it in every way I can that Canadian natural gas is used in Canada. I realize that today in Alberta wells have been drilled and capped. Well after well is sitting there idle, the gas not being used; and I understand that in many cases even the oil is not being used because, while the potential production is there, the market has not been developed.
The challenge to us today is to see to it that the market is developed, that the gas is allowed to flow-and that it is allowed to flow for the use of Canadians.

Mr. Speaker, in the light of the statement made by the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) a week or so ago in this debate perhaps it is not now as urgent as it might otherwise have been to require from the sponsors of the bill now before us the definite assurance for which those of us who have stood for the principle of Canada first have always asked, before we have been willing to let bills of this kind pass, namely the assurance that the main line for the transportation of gas would be built through Canada before crossing into the United States. We have also asked for the assurance that Canadian needs, wherever they might exist and wherever they might be served potentially by the gas transported in the pipe line, would be served, before any export was permitted to the United States.
Nevertheless, while the Minister of Trade and Commerce has now enunciated clearly the policy that he will not grant a permit for the export of natural gas which comes to the east until the needs of eastern Canada are met, I still think there are certain things that should be drawn to the attention of the house in connection with the bill, and there are certain assurances we should still ask from the sponsors of the bill before it is allowed to .pass.
I submit to you, sir, that the position of British Columbia members as related to this bill is as vitally affected as in connection with earlier bills before the house which had for their purpose the incorporation of IMr. Adamson.]

companies to transmit natural gas from the Alberta fields to the Pacific -coast. As I shall show a little later in my remarks, I believe there is a real danger that if the gas from the Alberta wells which is moved eastward by way of pipe lines, instead of going to Ontario and Quebec, is diverted to supply the American market at Chicago, Minneapolis or some other point in that area, not only will Ontario and Quebec be deprived of any supply of gas, but the interior portion of British Columbia will find itself in a similar position and, as a result, will never have a supply of Canadian natural gas.
I suggest to you, sir, that the interests of British Columbia members, like those of most hon. members, are not only bound up in the broad general principle of Canada first, for which those of us in this party have never hesitated to fight, but are also immediately concerned with the welfare and the economy of our own province.
Before developing that argument however I should like to make it clear that, in respect of this matter of the eastward movement of gas, the party to which I have the honour to belong takes the same position it has taken throughout the years, the same -position it has taken since the incorporation of gas and oil pipe line companies came before the house in 1949. Our position is that parliament must ensure that the Canada first policy is pursued, so that the needs of Canada will first be served. If I may say so without offence, even although I think he may not altogether welcome the compliment, I am glad to be able to record the conversion of the Minister of Trade and Commerce to that policy.

In those cases we tried to ensure that before Alberta gas moving westward went into the United States it should go through Canada-in those instances the portion of

Canada affected was British Columbia-and we take the same position here. Perhaps I should complete the picture by reminding you that we have been successful. It appears now that the only company which is going to get a permit to export Alberta gas to the Pacific -coast is the Westcoast Transmission Company which is going to build its line through British Columbia to serve the southern interior of that province before reaching Vancouver, and then if its present application to Washington is successful it will proceed into the United States to serve the Pacific northwestern states of Washington and Oregon.
Here we have an extension or, if you like, a counterpart of that policy. I think that, as a measure of gratitude for the co-operation a few eastern members gave to British Columbia in that connection, we are bound to take the same position with regard to the bill before us and insist that Alberta gas moving east should serve Canadian needs before being exported to the United States.
So that there may be no misunderstanding, let me reiterate that the policy of this party is not and never has been a Canada only policy. In other words, this party would not deny the export of surplus gas or oil to the United States. That has never been and is not now the policy of this party. The policy rather is that Canadian needs must be served first before the surplus, if any, is exported beyond our borders.
In this connection I must confess that I found the position of the Social Credit party as enunciated by their leader in this house a little difficult to understand. I must say also that I found their position, during the earlier controversies when we were fighting in connection with the westward movement of gas on the basis that Canada should be served first before the line entered the United States, a little difficult to understand.

speechtext:
As the parliamentary
assistant will recall, I raised this very same point in the committee, about the excessive amount. I repeat that I hold no brief for foreign vessel owners who may break this law but, as the parliamentary assistant will realize, there are possibilities within the

ambit of this law that certain Canadian vessels and Canadian masters may be involved. For instance, if a Canadian master or sailor, under section 7(d), resisted or wilfully obstructed a protection officer in, the execution of his duty he would immediately become liable for the fine provided by subsection 2 of section 8:
(a)	upon conviction on indictment to a fine of ten thousand dollars or to imprisonment for a term of one year or to both fine and imprisonment, or
(b)	upon summary conviction to a fine of two thousand dollars or to imprisonment for a term of one month or to both fine and imprisonment.
If we compare, Mr. Chairman, the penalties provided under the Criminal Code, as it now stands, for resisting and wilfully obstructing a peace officer on land, we find that under section 168, when the offence is triable by indictment, the offender would be subject to a maximum penalty of two years' imprisonment. If the offence is tried summarily, the offender would be subject to a term not exceeding six months' imprisonment or to a fine not exceeding $200. It seems to me that there is a wide margin between the two offences which are, in effect, the same offence in the eyes of the law, except that one is committed on land and the other on the sea. When we consider that the penalty under the Code of $200 for the same offence is increased fifty times, that is up to $10,000 under the bill which we are now studying-furthermore, the penalty provided under the old section 13 of the Customs and Fisheries Protection Act, which the present bill is to replace, was $800, and this penalty is being increased twenty-five times under the present statute- then, I submit, these increases are far-reaching.
Again I say that, were it not for the fact that some of our Canadian seamen and masters would be liable under this section, I would not stand up and raise these objections. It is in order to protect possible offenders, Canadian seamen and masters, that I rise to bring this to the attention of the parliamentary assistant. When we increase a penalty by fifty times or by twenty-five times, we are certainly going some. I submit that these penalties should be revised, especially so far as they may relate to Canadian seamen or masters.

subsubtopic: PROTECTION OP COASTAL FISHERIES
speechtext:
I think the purpose of this bill is to protect Canadian coastal fisheries and to protect Canadian coastal fishermen, not to protect the law-breaker whether or not he be a Canadian coastal fisherman. If you are going to have small fines in these sections, they could become nothing more or less than licence fees for breaking the law. With the modern fishing vessels that are in

use today, a fine of $200 or $300 would be just another small item of expense which might be cheerfully charged up in connection with an infraction of the law which would enable them to make an illegal catch worth thousands of dollars.
If it is a fact that the penalty has gone up from twenty-five to fifty times what it used to be, I would point out that the catch of the modern fishing vessel has gone up twenty-five to fifty times over the small hand-operated dories that were at one time in use on the east coast and to a lesser extent on the west coast. We have heard so many complaints, time after time, in connection with the administration of laws of this kind, that we do not put teeth in them so as to make them a deterrent to the law-breaker. Here is a section with ample protection in the words "not exceeding", and the high penalties are only imposed after a trial on indictment which means a trial by jury. If we are going to endeavour to administer that law with such small penalties that anyone can cheerfully break the law, pay the penalty and still be money ahead, our law is not going to be effective at all.

I should like to make a very brief comment on this bill before it passes. I did not have an opportunity of being present when the bill was discussed in the committee stage, but as I view it the most important element appears to give the government the power to extend what we ordinarily term the three-mile limit. This power is, I think, written into the bill in such a way that the limit, I trust, will not be extended in any arbitrary fashion because the consequences of dealing with it in that manner can be very dangerous indeed. We have seen what happened in Iceland recently. The Icelandic people decided to extend their three-mile limit to four miles and block off the British trawlers. As a result, the British refused to buy any fish from Iceland. The fish from Iceland was then sent to the market in the United States in considerable quantit'' and as the parliamentary assistant knows even at this special season of the year there is a glut of fish. The fish from Newfoundland cannot be sold at the present time except at a very great loss.
I point this out for one reason only. Because of the action the Icelandic people took, without a proper discussion with the British people and others engaged in that fishery, this situation evolved. Now, the fishery with which Newfoundland is primarily concerned is the Grand Banks. At the present time there is grave danger of the banks being depleted. A wish has been expressed in this house, I believe by the hon. member for Trinity-Conception (Mr. Stick), that the limit be extended. I want to suggest to the parliamentary assistant, and through him to the minister, that no action of this kind be taken without a very full discussion with all those engaged in that type of fishery. At the present time you have the various nationalities, and if you start imposing this kind of rule you may very well start some kind of chain reaction the same as occurred in Iceland. I merely pass that along for the consideration of the parliamentary assistant. I would not like to see all the Portuguese and Spaniards prevented from fishing. They are old historic markets, and a lot of trouble could be made for various Canadian fisheries by any ill-considered action of this kind. While the power will be in this act, I feel sure it will be exercised in a very sensible manner.

speakeroldname: Mr. T. G. W. Ashbourne (Grand Falls-While Bay):
subsubtopic: PROTECTION OP COASTAL FISHERIES

In endorsing and supporting third reading of this bill I should like to point out that in addition to the cod fisheries, which have just been mentioned by the hon. member for St. John's East (Mr. Higgins),

Coastal Fisheries
on the east coast of Newfoundland, we have a very important seal fishery, which is being prosecuted by vessels from Newfoundland at the present time, ana also I believe, one from Halifax and several Norwegian steamers as well. I should like to point out to the house the importance of this seal fishery. These seals, hundreds of thousands of them, some think there are millions of them, or a million anyway, are very important to Newfoundland and Canada. They constitute a very important industry. To protect such an industry as the sealing industry as well as the cod fishery it is important that the government should take powers to conserve this very important fishery primarily for the Canadian people. Around our shores these fish are found in vast numbers. We readily understand of course that other people have to eat as well, and when we see the Spaniards, the French, the Italians and the Portuguese, as well as others, coming over seeking food, we know they are looking after the requirements and the needs of their people. But I speak particularly at this time because quite a few Newfoundlanders are out on the stormy deep tonight prosecuting the seal fishery. I am glad to say, aided by the aeroplane which the operators have hired to go out, they have been able to locate two or three patches of seals.
These seals are sometimes found in the gulf of St. Lawrence, but owing to the mildness of the winter this year I understand there are very few seals in the gulf. Some of the ships that sailed from St. John's that were going to operate in the gulf went through the strait of Belle Isle, and I have been informed that they have struck one or two of the patches, or probably the main patch, on the east coast. These seals whelp on the ice early in March and they are in the main in two patches. There is the hood seal, which is a very valuable seal, and also the harp seal. The young harps have white coats on them and long hair, and they are sought after for their hides as well as the oil in them.
In the past it has been a very remunerative source of income to Newfoundland. Many years ago as many as 600,000 seals were obtained in a season, tout in the last few years not so many have been obtained, although in my time from 150,000 to 200,000 seals were brought in during one season. I just mention this, Mr. Speaker, to emphasize the importance of this fishery, particularly as the seals come down from the coast of Labrador, and gradually are brought down nearer the Grand Banks on the ice floes.
When we realize that it pays the Norwegians to send their ships over to prosecute this fishery, naturally its importance is quite evident to us here in Canada. The government has done well to introduce the legislation which has been passed through the house tonight, and which was considered in committee. When the regulations are drawn up and they can be readily used to protect our people I believe that they will be a very strong bargaining point, and through them we shall be able to do more trade with the Spaniards and the Portuguese, and with the Portuguese particularly, because the amount of fish they have bought from Newfoundland this year is under 50,000 quintals; whereas last year they purchased something over 100,000 quintals and the year before that about 170,000 quintals. Therefore I congratulate the government on bringing down this legislation and believe that it will be very helpful to the people of Newfoundland and to the people of the rest of Canada.

speakeroldname: Mr. Paul E. Cote (Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Labour):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Labour
subsubtopic: REVISION OF RATES OF COMPENSATION TO DISABLED SEAMEN
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this bill provides for amendments to the Merchant Seamen Compensation Act, which was passed by parliament in 1946. That act replaced and largely embodied the provisions of the merchant seamen compensation regulations of 1945, passed under the authority of the War Measures Act.
The act provides for payment of compensation to seamen who are injured in the course of their employment, and to dependents of seamen who are killed in the course of their employment, and who are not covered in respect of the accident under any provincial workmen's compensation act.
A seaman who cannot claim compensation under any provincial compensation act is eligible therefore to claim for benefits under the Merchant Seamen Compensation Act, if he is employed on a ship of Canadian registry, or one under charter to a person resident in Canada or having his principal place of business in Canada if the ship is on a foreign or "home trade voyage". I might explain that a home trade voyage covers coastal trade voyages and is defined in the Canada Shipping Act, but does not include a voyage on inland waters in Canada; a foreign trade voyage is a voyage extending beyond the limits of a home trade voyage.
The amendments are very simple. They provide for an upward revision in the scale of benefits payable under the act, having regard for the changes in the seamen's earnings and changes in living conditions which have occurred in the past several years since the passage of the act.
Merchant Seamen Compensation Act
Under the present provisions of the act, claims are not considered where an accident does not result in disabling a seaman from earning full wages for seven days. We propose to reduce this period to four days. It is also proposed to raise the ceiling of yearly earnings for use in the computation of compensation from $2,500 to $3,600.
The significant changes in cash benefits which are provided in the bill are as follows:
1.	The maximum payment towards the funeral expenses of a deceased seaman is increased from $125 to $200;
2.	The amount of the monthly allowance or pension to the widow of a deceased seaman is increased from $45 to $50, and the same increase applies in the case of an invalid husband who was dependent on the earnings of a deceased wife employed on a ship;
3.	Where there are dependent children as well as a widow or invalid husband, the monthly payment for each child under 18 years of age is to be increased from $10 to $15 and, in the event of the death of the widowed mother or invalid father, the monthly amount paid to the dependent children is increased from $20 to $25 for each child;
4.	In the case of a deceased seaman who leaves no widow but leaves dependent children under 18 years of age, the monthly payment to each child is increased from $20 to $25.
I should explain at this point that the act provides that the total compensation payable to the widow and children of a deceased seaman is not to exceed in any event the average earnings of the seaman prior to his decease.
5.	The minimum amount of compensation to which an injured seaman is entitled for temporary total or permanent total disability which is now fixed at $12.50 per week or the sum equivalent to the seaman's earnings if less than that, is increased to a minimum of $15 per week, or a sum equivalent to the seaman's earnings if less than that.
On January 1, 1950, the responsibility for administering the act which previously had been vested in the Minister of Transport (Mr. Chevrier) was transferred to the Minister of Labour (Mr. Gregg) by virtue of an order in council passed under the Public Service Rearrangement and Transfer of Duties Act. This transfer of administration is given statutory effect in the amendments to the act contained in this bill.
Since the act came into force, or I should say since the regulations of 1945 were made effective, there have been 578 accidents reported as coming under the regulations or act. The number has been declining year
3168	HOUSE OF
Merchant Seamen Compensation Act by year because the employing shipping companies covered by the act have decreased in number from 102 in 1947 to 66 in the last fiscal year. Their number has now increased to 90 as of this date.
Our act covers seamen on ships of Canadian registry or operated by companies or persons with chief place of business in Canada. There has been a switch from Canadian to other registry to account for the decrease I have mentioned. This decrease has been counteracted in the current fiscal year by an influx of new registrations, mainly from Newfoundland.
As hon. members will know, we do not pay any compensation from federal funds. By the act, shipping companies are required to place the necessary liability insurance to cover the risks of compensation arising under the act. Payments of compensation by a company under the act are covered by the insurance policy.
The claims for compensation arising under the act are adjudicated by a board known as the merchant seamen compensation board composed of three officers of the public service.
Cost of administration was $3,463 in the fiscal year 1951-52. Every employer coming under our act pays $25 a year, and there is an additional assessment on companies whose employees suffer accidents. This is an amount based on the number of such accidents, and equals the balance of cost of administration over and above that collected through the annual $25 assessment.
We think this is a worth-while amendment to the act, even if it does apply only to relatively few people. It is necessary for the protection of our seamen and their dependents. I am sure it will commend itself to the house.

speechtext: Does the parliamentary assistant consider that the provision for $50 a month for a widow, as set out in section 3(2)(d), is sufficient? It states that where the widow or an invalid husband is the sole dependent, there shall be a monthly payment of $50. It seems to me that is entirely too low a compensation at today's living costs. Upon what standard did the department base that figure? What standard do they accept in order to establish $50 as being adequate compensation for a widow under these conditions?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Labour
subsubtopic: REVISION OF RATES OF COMPENSATION TO DISABLED SEAMEN
speechtext: I agree with the hon. member that this amount is certainly not excessive, but it compares with the monthly pensions to widows in all provinces except Saskatchewan and British Columbia where the amounts are $60 and $75 respectively.

subsubtopic: REVISION OF RATES OF COMPENSATION TO DISABLED SEAMEN
speechtext: Could not the minister, the department and the federal government set a standard for those provinces which the parliamentary assistant admits make too low a payment? If that is the basis on which they have established this payment of $50, why should not the federal government and this parliament set a standard for those provinces which are considered to be too low?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Labour
subsubtopic: REVISION OF RATES OF COMPENSATION TO DISABLED SEAMEN
speechtext: Workmen's compensation legislation is under the jurisdiction of the provinces. This is intended to be supplementary to the workmen's compensation coverage. If our rates compare favourably with those of the provinces I think under those circumstances we could hardly be blamed.

subsubtopic: REVISION OF RATES OF COMPENSATION TO DISABLED SEAMEN
speechtext: I understand that under the British North America Act shipping and navigation is the responsibility of the federal government and therefore we should be setting a standard, by providing adequate compensation for these widows, for those provinces where the payments are admitted to be too low.

subsubtopic: REVISION OF RATES OF COMPENSATION TO DISABLED SEAMEN
speechtext:
I think the rate of $50 is
too low. The $45 which was paid in 1946 was really a larger amount than the $50 being suggested here. However, I must agree with the parliamentary assistant that the payments provided in the bill are not out of line with the average payments in the provinces. In Saskatchewan the payment for a child under sixteen years of age is $25, and this bill provides for a payment of $25 for each child under the age of eighteen years.
Perhaps a better way of providing for compensation to be paid for merchant seamen would be to put it on the basis of what is paid in the province where the ship is registered. That would give seamen on ships running out of Vancouver or Victoria a slightly better compensation than is provided under this bill. However, the difference would not be so great. I insist again that $50 today has much less purchasing power than $45 in 1946.

subsubtopic: REVISION OF RATES OF COMPENSATION TO DISABLED SEAMEN
speechtext:
I do not
think the parliamentary assistant has answered the argument. If $45 was considered by the dominion government in 1946 as being suitable compensation, how can it justify a payment of $50 today? The cost of


living has increased at least 90 per cent and I submit that there should be a higher payment for widows.
Take the case of a ship that goes down with all hands. The captain may be getting $500 a month, the first engineer $400 a month and so on down the line; yet the widow of every man lost will receive the same amount, namely, $50. Is that compensation for the loss which she has sustained? In times of war many ships have gone down and the widows of all the men who are lost are paid the same $50. I suggest that that is most inadequate. If the federal government is the supreme authority in the country it should set a good example.
It would take at least $75 to equal the $45 that was paid in 1946. It would not cost the federal government anything because they are going to be insured. It must be obvious to everyone that this is only a sideline for the Department of Labour or whatever department is handling it. Nobody seems to know what department is really handling it because there is one man from the Department of Labour and another man from the maritime commission. It is not receiving the attention that it deserves.
I admit that it is a good thing as far as it goes, but it does not go far enough. I suggest that greater attention be given to this in the coming year with special attention being paid to the amount of compensation to widows and to those who are engaged in this arduous occupation.
When replying to the hon. member for Charlotte reference was made by the parliamentary assistant to fishermen who go out from their home ports to the fishing grounds and then back in again and also to those fishermen who undertake long voyages to the north pole or to the south pole or into waters where they are more apt to meet with violent storms. It is not possible for them to run for a safe harbour when they receive a weather report that is unfavourable.
I have seen 60 or 70 vessels coming off the banks at one time because foul weather was reported. But when you are crossing the Atlantic to Liverpool or on some other long voyage you cannot do that; you must face what comes. Therefore they should receive a higher basic compensation.
